    target_compile_definitions(${exercise} PRIVATE EXERCISM_TEST_SUITE)

if(${MSVC})
    set_target_properties(${exercise} PROPERTIES
        COMPILE_DEFINITIONS_DEBUG _SCL_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS
        COMPILE_FLAGS "/WX /w44244 /w44267")
endif()

# Run the tests on every build
add_custom_target(test_${exercise} ALL DEPENDS ${exercise} COMMAND ${exercise})

part.text:
The solution is implemented, but shell commands were denied so I couldn't compile and run the tests myself. Here's what I wrote:

**`perfect_numbers.h`** — declares the `classification` enum (`perfect`, `abundant`, `deficient`) and `classification classify(int number)`, with `<stdexcept>` included for `std::domain_error`.

**`perfect_numbers.cpp`** — `classify` throws `std::domain_error` for `number <= 0`, then computes the aliquot sum by scanning divisors from 2 up to `√number`, adding both factors `i` and `number/i` (skipping the duplicate when `i² == number`). `1` gets an aliquot sum of 0. It then compares the sum to the number to return the right classification.

To verify, you can run:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DEXERCISM_RUN_ALL_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build
./build/perfect-numbers
```

The implementation covers all test cases: perfect (6, 28, 33550336), abundant (12, 30, 33550335), deficient (2, 4, 32, 33550337, 1), and `domain_error` for 0 and -1. The divisor loop runs in O(√n), so it handles the large test values quickly.
